_meta.purpose: The Pit Log house recipe canon. Every recipe the brief names (section 10) and every recipe an approved graphic promises by name. NONE is OFFICIAL. A recipe becomes TEST_V1 when it has been written in full with quantities, TEST_V2+ after each kitchen test, and OFFICIAL only after a documented kitchen test signed off by Anthony. Until a recipe reaches at least TEST_V1 and has a live page, any graphic that names it is blocked from publication (graphics/masters.json publish_gate).

recipes.title: Pit Log Central Texas Brisket
recipes.description: Salt, coarse black pepper, post oak, patience. A whole packer smoked at 250 F, wrapped in butcher paper through the stall, pulled probe tender, and rested long above 140 F.
concept_ingredients: optional: Pit Log House Brisket Rub
recipes.prep_time: 30 minutes to trim. Add an overnight dry brine if you have the time.
recipes.cook_time_guidance: 10 to 16 hours at 250 F, plus a 1 to 2 hour rest. Estimate. Start earlier than you think.

items.item: whole packer brisket, 12 to 14 lb, untrimmed

items.note: 16 mesh if you can find it
optional. Central Texas purists skip it.

steps: Trim. Leave a quarter inch of fat on the cap. Cut out the hard fat between the point and the flat. Round the edges so nothing burns.
Mix the rub. Coat every side. If you have the time, leave it uncovered in the fridge overnight.
Run the pit at 250 F. Post oak, clean thin smoke. Put the brisket on fat side up, point toward the fire.
Leave it alone for 4 hours. Then spritz with water every hour if the edges look dry.

The stall. Somewhere around 150 to 170 F the temperature stops climbing. It can sit there for hours. That is normal. When the bark is set and dark, usually 165 to 175 F, wrap it tight in butcher paper.

Back on at 250 F. Start checking at 195 F. It is done when a probe slides into the flat with almost no resistance. That is usually between 195 and 205 F. The number is a checkpoint. The feel is the answer. USDA FSIS calls beef safe at 145 F with a 3 minute rest. Brisket passed that hours ago. This window is about collagen, not safety.
Rest. Leave it wrapped on the counter for 30 minutes. Then hold it in a dry cooler or a 150 F oven for 1 to 2 hours. Keep it above 140 F the whole time. That is the USDA line for hot holding.
Slice the flat across the grain, pencil thick. Turn the point 90 degrees and slice it across its own grain, thicker. Serve on paper.
notes: Untested as a Pit Log recipe. This is the standard Central Texas method. It becomes OFFICIAL after a logged cook.
USDA FSIS calls beef safe at 145 F with a 3 minute rest. Brisket is not tender there. The 195 to 205 F window is about collagen, not safety.

recipes.title: Coffee-Chile Smoked Chuck Roast
recipes.description: A chuck roast treated like a small brisket with a coffee and ancho rub, wrapped at the stall and pulled probe tender for slicing or shredding.

recipes.title: Reverse-Seared Ribeye with Ember Butter
recipes.description: Thick ribeyes brought up slowly in smoke, then seared hard over coals and finished with a compound butter. Doneness is the cook's preference; the page prints the Beef Board scale and the USDA minimum side by side.
recipes.cook_time_guidance: 45 to 60 minutes in smoke plus a 2 minute sear. Planning estimate only.

recipes.title: Santa Maria-Inspired Tri-Tip
recipes.description: Garlic, salt, pepper and red oak. Smoked to just under the target, seared, rested, and sliced across both grain directions.
recipes.prep_time: 10 minutes, plus 1 hour uncovered in the fridge
recipes.cook_time_guidance: 60 to 90 minutes at 225 F, then a 2 to 3 minute sear per side, plus a 10 minute rest. Estimate.

items.item: tri-tip roast, 2 to 3 lb, fat cap trimmed to a quarter inch
red oak chunks, or any oak

steps: Mix the rub and coat the tri-tip on every side. Leave it uncovered in the fridge for an hour so the surface dries.
Run the pit at 225 F with oak. Red oak is the Santa Maria tradition. Tri-tip on, fat side up, leave-in probe in the thickest part.
Smoke until the probe reads about 10 F under your target. Roasts rise 5 to 15 F after they leave the heat (Beef Board), so for a 145 F medium rare final, pull around 130 to 135 F.
Sear over direct heat or in a hot cast iron pan, 2 to 3 minutes a side, until the crust is dark.

Rest 10 minutes. USDA FSIS calls beef safe at 145 F with a 3 minute rest. The Beef Board scale is medium rare 145 F, medium 160 F, well done 170 F, final temperatures after rest. Steakhouse convention pulls lower; that is a preference below the minimum, and the beef temperature page says so.
Find the two grain directions. Tri-tip changes grain at the bend. Cut the roast in two at the bend, then slice each half across its own grain, thin.
notes: Untested draft. Standard Santa Maria method; becomes OFFICIAL after a logged cook.
Tri-tip is a steak-style cut. Do not cook it to a brisket window; it dries out.

recipes.title: Pepper-Bark Beef Short Ribs
recipes.description: Plate short ribs with a heavy pepper bark, smoked unwrapped until probe tender between the bones.

recipes.title: Pit Log Ember Citrus BBQ Sauce
recipes.description: A bright, smoky house sauce built on ketchup, reduced apple juice, fresh orange juice, brown sugar, vinegar, molasses and warm spice. Made for brisket, short ribs and grilled beef.

items.note: reduced by half first, see step 1

steps: Pour the apple juice into a small pan. Simmer it over medium heat until it drops to about half a cup. That takes 8 to 10 minutes. It builds apple flavor without watering the sauce down.
Add everything else except the zest. Stir until the sugar dissolves.
Bring to a bare simmer. Cook uncovered for 20 minutes. Stir now and then. It is ready when it coats a spoon.
Stir in the zest. Taste it. Add vinegar if it is too sweet. Add brown sugar if it bites.
Cool it, then jar it. It keeps in the fridge for 2 weeks.
On the pit, brush it on in the last 15 to 30 minutes. The sugar sets and does not burn. That is the USDA FSIS timing for sauce on smoked meat.
notes: Untested draft. Concept from the approved Pit Log beef graphic. The amounts are a first pass. They will move after the first kitchen test.
Built for brisket, short ribs and grilled beef. Thin it with a splash of the reduced apple juice to use it as a mop.

recipes.title: Pit Log Carolina Gold Mustard Sauce
recipes.description: A tangy South Carolina mustard sauce: yellow mustard, apple cider vinegar, brown sugar, honey, Worcestershire, garlic and black pepper. For pulled pork, ribs and chops.
steps: Whisk everything together in a small pan.
Bring it to a bare simmer over medium-low heat. Cook 10 to 15 minutes and keep stirring. It thickens a little and the raw vinegar edge softens.
Cool it. It thickens more as it cools. Keeps in the fridge for 2 weeks.
Serve it at the table with pulled pork. Or brush it on ribs and chops in the last 15 to 30 minutes on the pit.
notes: Untested draft. Concept from the approved Pit Log pork graphic. South Carolina style: mustard first, sugar second.
Skip the honey and add one more tablespoon of vinegar for a sharper version.

recipes.title: Pit Log Smoked Chicken Thighs
recipes.description: Simple rub, low and slow, hot finish for the skin. Olive oil, garlic, paprika, smoked paprika, brown sugar, salt and black pepper.

recipes.title: Pit Log Honey Garlic Chicken Thighs
recipes.description: Sweet, savoury, smoky. Chicken thighs, honey, soy sauce, garlic, brown sugar, apple cider vinegar and paprika. Glaze goes on in the last 15 to 30 minutes (FSIS).
recipes.prep_time: 15 minutes, plus 30 minutes in the fridge with the rub if you have it
recipes.cook_time_guidance: 1.5 to 2 hours at 275 F, then a short hot finish. Estimate.

items.item: bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs, about 3 lb

steps: Pat the thighs dry. Mix the salt, paprika, pepper and garlic powder. Rub it on every side and under the skin where you can. Fridge, uncovered, 30 minutes if you have the time.
Whisk the glaze in a small pan. Simmer 3 to 4 minutes until it thickens a little. Set half aside for the table.
Run the pit at 275 F with cherry or pecan. Skin side up. Leave the lid shut for an hour.
Brush on the glaze in the last 15 to 30 minutes. That is the USDA FSIS timing for sauce on smoked meat, and it keeps the honey from burning.

Check the innermost part of each thigh, not touching bone. USDA FSIS says all chicken is safe at 165 F. Thighs eat better at 175 to 185 F, when the connective tissue has rendered. That extra is texture, not safety.
For crisp skin, move the thighs over direct heat or into a 400 F oven for 3 to 5 minutes at the end.
Rest 5 minutes. USDA requires no rest for poultry; this one is for juice. Serve with the reserved glaze.
notes: Untested draft. Concept from the approved Pit Log chicken graphic. Amounts are a first pass.
Boneless thighs work too. They finish sooner, so start checking at the one-hour mark.

recipes.title: Mediterranean Lamb Shoulder
recipes.description: Herb-marinated, smoked low and slow until fall-apart tender. Olive oil, garlic, lemon, rosemary, thyme, oregano, sea salt and black pepper.
recipes.yield: A 5 to 6 lb bone-in shoulder serves 6 to 8
recipes.prep_time: 20 minutes, plus 4 hours to overnight in the marinade
recipes.cook_time_guidance: 6 to 8 hours at 250 F, wrapped for the last half, plus a 30 to 60 minute rest. Estimate.
steps: Score the fat cap in a diamond pattern, a quarter inch deep. Mix the marinade and rub it into every cut and under any loose flaps.
Bag it or cover it and marinate in the refrigerator, 4 hours to overnight. Never on the counter. USDA FSIS: marinate in the fridge and discard the used marinade.
Run the pit at 250 F with oak, or oak and cherry. Shoulder on fat side up. Leave it alone for 3 hours.
When the bark is set and dark, usually 160 to 170 F, wrap tight in butcher paper. Back on at 250 F.

Start checking at 195 F. It is done when a probe slides into the thickest part, away from the blade bone, with almost no resistance. That is usually 195 to 205 F. USDA FSIS calls lamb safe at 145 F with a 3 minute rest; this cook passed that hours ago. The extra is about collagen, not safety.
Rest wrapped for 30 to 60 minutes. Keep it above 140 F if you hold it longer.
Pull it off the bone with forks or claws. Squeeze fresh lemon over it. Serve on flatbread with yogurt, or over rice.
notes: Untested draft. Concept from the approved Pit Log lamb graphic.
For a sliced roast instead of pulled, follow the American Lamb Board scale on the lamb temperature page: pull at 135 F for a 145 F medium rare after rest.

recipes.title: Moroccan Spiced Goat Shoulder
recipes.description: Bold, aromatic, fall-apart tender. Harissa, cumin, coriander, garlic, lemon, olive oil, paprika and cinnamon. Smoke, then wrap or braise, because goat is lean (FSIS).
recipes.yield: A 4 to 5 lb bone-in shoulder serves 5 to 6
recipes.prep_time: 20 minutes, plus 4 hours to overnight in the paste
recipes.cook_time_guidance: 5 to 7 hours at 240 F, wrapped with liquid for the second half, plus a 30 minute rest. Estimate.

items.item: heavy foil, or a Dutch oven

steps: Mix the paste. Rub it over the whole shoulder and into every seam. Refrigerate, covered, 4 hours to overnight. USDA FSIS: marinate in the fridge, never on the counter.
Run the pit at 240 F with oak, or oak and a little pecan. Goat is lean; keep the pit gentle. Shoulder on for about 3 hours, until the paste has set into a crust.

Move the shoulder to a foil pan or a Dutch oven. Pour in the stock. Cover tight. Back on the pit, or into a 275 F oven. USDA FSIS says less tender goat cuts should be braised or stewed, and this is the braise.

Start checking after 2 more hours. It is done when a probe slides into the thickest meat, away from the blade bone, with almost no resistance, usually 195 to 205 F. USDA FSIS calls goat safe at 145 F with a 3 minute rest; this cook passed that long ago. The extra is about collagen.
Rest, covered, 30 minutes. Keep it above 140 F if you hold it longer.
Pull the meat and toss it in the pan juices. Finish with lemon and chopped cilantro or parsley. Serve over couscous or rice.
notes: Untested draft. Concept from the approved Pit Log goat graphic.
Harissa heat varies by brand. Taste the paste before it goes on and cut it with more olive oil if it is fierce.

recipes.title: Pit Log Maple Cedar Salmon
recipes.description: Sweet, smoky, balanced, on a soaked cedar plank. Maple syrup, Dijon mustard, soy sauce, garlic, lemon juice and smoked paprika. The page prints 145 F as the federal minimum and labels anything lower as preference.
recipes.prep_time: 15 minutes, plus 1 hour to soak the plank
recipes.cook_time_guidance: 15 to 20 minutes on a plank at 350 F, or 45 to 60 minutes smoked at 225 F. Estimate.
steps: Soak the plank in water for at least 1 hour. Weigh it down so it stays under.
Whisk the glaze. Set a third of it aside for serving.
Pat the salmon dry. Lay it skin down on the plank. Brush on half of the rest of the glaze.
Grill: heat to 350 F, indirect. Put the plank on and close the lid. Smoker: run 225 F with alder or apple.
Brush on the rest of the glaze after 10 minutes on the grill, or after 30 minutes in the smoker.

Check the thickest part with a thermometer through the side. USDA FSIS and FDA say 145 F, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes with a fork. Many cooks pull it earlier for a softer center. That is a preference below the federal minimum, and this page says so.
Rest 3 to 5 minutes on the plank. Spoon the reserved glaze over the top. Serve from the board.
notes: Untested draft. Concept from the approved Pit Log salmon graphic.
Cedar planks are one use on the grill. Rinse and reuse only for low smoking.
